Our results based on 24 pairs suggest that Sclater’s Wrens have sexually dimorphic songs, and that both females and males combine their songs to produce duets. column7: "Babble-Singing, Soft Singing, Whisper Song, and Rhythmic Singing. Often accompanied by raised head and flashing of white nictitating membrane; usually uttered only by males. Probably the equivalent of song in other passerines; can be heard from only about 50 m (Baeyens 1979a). Dominant Black-billed Magpies often approach predator, or even human intruder, and challenge it by Babble-Singing in self-assertive manner; described as “cheeky” behavior by Birkhead (Birkhead 1991), when directed toward him. Often starts with soft chatters of 1 or 2 notes; then gradually progresses into whistled subsong of 6–7 syllables. For a sonogram of this and several other calls, see Birkhead 1991: 68. This challenging or assertive behavior given around predators has never been observed in European magpies (Birkhead 1991). Soft Singing is uttered quietly, usually by courting males; similar Whisper Song is given by both sexes during nest-building (Cramp and Perrins 1994a). Louder Rhythmic Singing also given by males during courtship. Both Soft Singing and Rhythmic Singing sound like subsongs. Rhythmic Singing seems more rigid in sequence and stereotyped than Babble-Singing. Babble-Singing is often given by young, aggressive males, but a wild adult female was heard to give this varied whistlelike song while sitting alone in a flight cage (CHT), and young magpies between 6 and 20 wk old have been heard uttering this call (Cramp and Perrins 1994a).
